item.title: How Ancient Farmers Used Floral Designs to Track Goods
item.description: A Mesopotamian culture’s decorated ceramics show some early roots of math, researchers argued.
item.dc:creator: Franz Lidz

item.title: Early Data Indicates an A.I.-Generated Drug Could Slow Aging
item.description: Artificial intelligence was used to help develop a drug candidate, rentosertib, for a rare lung condition. Its maker says the drug also seems to reduce the biological hallmarks of age.
item.dc:creator: Cade Metz
item.media:description: Rentosertib, Insilico Medicine’s small-molecule drug candidate developed and designed using generative A.I. for treating chronic lung disease, at the company’s research and development facility in Shanghai.

item.title: The 92-Year-Old Mathematician and the Teenage Apprentice
item.description: Joan Birman thought her major discoveries were behind her. Then came an email from a young neighbor — a girl who knew little but wanted to learn.
item.dc:creator: Gregory Barber
item.media:credit: Oliver Farshi for The New York Times

item.title: Inside the D.O.J.’s Investigation of Fauci and Other Virus Scientists
item.description: As Dr. Anthony Fauci has faced public scrutiny from congressional Republicans, the D.O.J. has pursued a quieter and more expansive effort against a wider circle of researchers.
item.dc:creator: Benjamin Mueller and Glenn Thrush
item.category: National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases
item.media:description: President Trump and Dr. Anthony S. Fauci were shown models of the coronavirus during a tour of the National Institutes of Health in March 2020.

item.title: Is There Alien Debris on the Moon? Some Scientists Plan to Find Out.
item.description: Researchers want to explore the idea that microscopic particles shed by alien civilizations have accumulated on the lunar surface, making it an archive of extraterrestrial technology.
item.dc:creator: Becky Ferreira
item.media:description: Harrison H. Schmitt, an Apollo 17 astronaut, on his way to take samples on the lunar surface in 1972. Scientists propose sending a lunar mission to sift through about a cubic meter of soil to screen for materials.

item.title: The World’s First Bugs Had Way More Legs
item.description: Meet the earliest known insects. Shaking hands with them will take a while.
item.dc:creator: Kate Golembiewski

item.title: Scientists Find More Than 1,000 DNA Variants Linked to Personality Traits
item.description: More than one million genomes helped identify DNA variants linked to extroversion, agreeableness, neuroticism and more. Researchers measured how those traits influenced how people lived.
item.dc:creator: Emily Baumgaertner Nunn

item.title: What Did Jurassic Forests Sound Like? Like This.
item.description: Scientists spent over a decade reconstructing the calls of nine species of ancient insects to create the first accurate Jurassic soundscape.
item.dc:creator: Annie Roth
item.category: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
item.media:description: By studying the fossilized wings of ancient insects as well as the bioacoustics of their living relatives, researchers were able to use computer modeling and machine learning to replicate their sounds.

item.title: Scientists Hunting Dark Matter Found Something Strange
item.description: A lone signal from an experiment in South Dakota doesn’t fit the profile of any other known particles, physicists say.
item.dc:creator: Katrina Miller

item.title: Top Mathematician Announces New Institute for A.I. Safety
item.description: Jacob Tsimerman, a recent recipient of the Fields Medal, believes that higher mathematics can help curb the dangers of runaway artificial intelligence.
item.dc:creator: Siobhan Roberts
item.media:description: Canadian mathematician Jacob Tsimerman, who has announced the founding of the Mathematical A.I. Safety Institute (MAISI).

item.title: A Newer Kind of Gene Editing Promises to Edit ‘Nurture’ Over ‘Nature’
item.description: Traditional gene editing rewrites DNA. But a new approach, called epigenome editing, aims to treat the molecular scars we collect throughout our lives.
item.dc:creator: Emily Baumgaertner Nunn

item.title: The Heart Drug Pelacarsen Fails, Shocking Novartis and Cardiologists
item.description: Doctors were hopeful the drug, which was being tested in a large clinical trial by Novartis, was going to be a powerful new tool to fight heart disease.
item.dc:creator: Gina Kolata
item.media:description: An illustration of lipoprotein(a), a low-density lipoprotein. Every study short of a randomized clinical trial had indicated that the drug would lower Lp(a) and help protect people from heart disease.

item.title: Pentagon Agreement With N.I.H. on Biodefense Draws Alarm From Democrats
item.description: Under a new partnership, the Defense Department would play a larger role in biodefense and pandemic preparedness. Democrats warned it could allow a Pentagon cash grab.
item.dc:creator: Catie Edmondson and Carolyn Y. Johnson
item.category: United States Defense and Military Forces
National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases
item.media:description: The agreement, a copy of which was obtained by The New York Times, is focused on chemical and biological defense research.

item.title: Hideki Shirakawa, Who Helped Turn a Lab Error Into a Nobel, Dies at 90
item.description: The Japanese chemist played a key role in the discovery of electricity-conducting plastics, largely by accident.
item.dc:creator: Dylan Loeb McClain
item.media:description: Hideki Shirakawa in Stockholm in 2000, when he shared the Nobel Prize. From a young age, he developed an ambition to work in the lab with plastics.

item.title: Plumbing the Shipwrecks of an Infamous Pirate Cove
item.description: For the marine archaeologist Sean Kingsley, the most honest history can be found on the seafloor.
item.dc:creator: Franz Lidz
item.media:credit: David Shaw for The New York Times

item.title: The Brains of F1 Drivers Are Indeed Strange
item.description: They are moving too fast for the normal mind to keep up, but elite drivers have more densely packed brain cells where it counts and use their minds more efficiently.
item.dc:creator: Erik Vance

item.title: Psilocybin May Prevent Nerve Damage Caused by Chemotherapy, Study Finds
item.description: The preliminary research was conducted in mice, but scientists were optimistic the results would apply to humans. Clinical trials begin this month.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Jacobs
item.media:credit: Mason Trinca for The New York Times
item.media:description: There are no effective treatments for neuropathy, which causes pain, tingling and numbness in the hands and feet, and can force patients to scale back or halt chemotherapy when the discomfort becomes too much.

item.title: Cleaner Air, Smarter Toddlers
item.description: New research links climate policies to improved early-childhood development.
item.dc:creator: Claire Brown
item.media:description: Researchers at Columbia University followed more than a thousand children between 1998 and 2020, testing their cognitive development.

item.title: Patagonia Sues Trump Over Reduction of Bears Ears National Monument in Utah
item.description: The outdoor apparel maker joined environmental and Native American groups in challenging President Trump’s reduction of Bears Ears National Monument.
item.dc:creator: Maxine Joselow
item.media:description: Tourists at Muley Point, looking out on Monument Valley, in Bears Ears National Monument in Utah.

item.title: In Nepal and Tibet, Pollution on Glaciers Could Fuel More Flood Disasters
item.description: Darkened by soot from vehicles and factories, the region’s glaciers are absorbing more heat and melting at dangerous rates.
item.dc:creator: Hiroko Tabuchi
item.category: Far East, South and Southeast Asia and Pacific Areas
item.media:credit: Jason Gulley for The New York Times
item.media:description: A meltwater lake on the Ngozumpa Glacier in Nepal in 2025.

item.title: Inside the Fight Against a Flesh-Eating Fly in Mexico
item.description: For the first time in a year, the U.S.-Mexico border partly reopened to cattle imports following a screwworm infestation across the region. The battle against the flesh-eating fly has only just begun deep in Mexico.
item.dc:creator: James Wagner and Luis Antonio Rojas
item.media:credit: Luis Antonio Rojas for The New York Times
item.media:description: New World screwworm flies in a cage at a facility in Metapa, Mexico, that that produces sterile flies, which when released into the wild slowly reduce the population size.

item.title: U.N. Says World Will Miss Its 1.5-Degree Climate Target
item.description: Carbon removal combined with emissions reduction is the only remaining pathway to avert catastrophic levels of warming, a new report warns.
item.dc:creator: Chico Harlan

item.title: A Nearly 200-Year-Old Museum Known for Its T. Rex Faces Extinction
item.description: The Academy of Natural Sciences in Philadelphia, which is affiliated with Drexel University, cited attendance struggles and higher costs in its decision to close.
item.dc:creator: Neil Vigdor
item.media:description: The Academy of Natural Sciences in Philadelphia opened in 1828 and is known for its Dinosaur Hall.

item.title: A Data Center Backlash
item.description: Today we visit Pennsylvania, where there’s a high-stakes clash over A.I. jobs and the environment.
item.dc:creator: David Gelles
item.media:credit: Kristian Thacker for The New York Times
item.media:description: A rally against data centers at the Pennsylvania State Capitol in Harrisburg this summer.

item.title: Ada Yonath, Chemist and First Israeli Woman to Receive a Nobel, Dies at 87
item.description: Her mapping of the ribosome, which led to new designs for antibiotics, faced years of derision, as many scientists saw it as a dead-end effort.
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Kandell
item.media:description: Ada Yonath in 2009. Her work, once dismissed as impractical, ultimately earned her a share of the Nobel Prize in Chemistry that year and opened new pathways for designing antibiotics at a time when drug resistance has become a global threat.

item.title: New York Climate ‘Superfund’ Law Falls in Court
item.description: The court said the measure, which required energy companies to pay $75 billion to the state, conflicted with federal law.
item.dc:creator: Karen Zraick
item.media:credit: Cindy Schultz for The New York Times
item.media:description: Kathy Hochul, New York’s governor, signed the law in 2024 and several other states have considered similar measures.
